**Verdict:** Yes. Hormozi would tell you to admit your weaknesses up front, in the ad itself. He calls this "damaging admissions" and says it may be his favorite copywriting tactic. How you word it matters: put the flaw first, then "but", then the claim you want people to believe.

**Based on:** said it. He covers this directly in two videos and repeats it in his summary of rules.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Admitting a flaw makes the rest of the ad believable.** "you want to always own your flaws of course you have them of course your product isn't perfect say so" ([14 Years of Marketing Advice @ 12:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=750s)). The trade, in his words: "what you'll sacrifice in promise you'll gain in trust and trust trumps promise" and "I would rather always sacrifice promise to gain trust" ([@ 13:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=789s)).
- **Customers are already thinking about the flaw.** If you say it first, you get the credit for honesty. "the prospect is already thinking them but if you can claim them instead of them thinking them you acknowledge them gain trust and then when you make your statements they will believe you more" ([@ 15:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=939s)).
- **Honesty makes you stand out.** "if you want to stand out in a crowded marketplace tell the truth" ([@ 15:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=939s)).

**How to word it (his method)**
1. **List your flaws.** "write down all of the flaws all the things that people complain about the things that you know you could do better and claim them" ([@ 15:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=903s)).
2. **Use "true, damaging thing BUT claim".** "the statement that comes after the word but is the part that is the thing you want them to believe" ([@ 13:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=824s)).
   - His examples: "our websites are ugly as hell but they convert", "our systems are incredibly boring but they work" ([@ 15:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=903s)).
   - **Don't reverse the order.** Whatever comes after "but" is what people remember, so "these markers write four times longer than others but they smell like crap" ends up stressing the smell ([@ 14:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=866s)).
3. **Make it funny if you can.** "if you can do with humor you get even more bonus points". His sample ad: "our gym has honestly pretty terrible parking our AC is kind of on and off i don't have the best equipment but our sessions are more fun than everyone else's cuz it's all we've got" ([@ 15:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=939s)).
4. **If your offer sounds too good to be true, list the downsides before the benefits.** Advising a travel-coaching business whose prospects didn't believe its results, he suggested opening with: "Listen, before I tell you about the good, let me tell you about the bad." The point is that people "can self-qualify": the right buyers decide they can live with the downsides ([$12M Business for a Stranger @ 19:42](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=1182s), [@ 20:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=1214s)).

He pairs this with saying who the product is *not* for, which he calls "even more powerful than the original call out" ([@ 5:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=302s)). Something like "If you need X, this isn't for you" is both an admission and a filter.

**What would change his answer:** He doesn't name any exceptions. Two limits follow from his reasoning, but they're my inference:
- The admission has to be true. The whole point is to earn trust, so a staged or fake flaw defeats it.
- The flaw has to be something your ideal customer can live with. If the weakness breaks your main promise ("ugly but doesn't convert"), wording won't save it. That's a product problem, and he'd tell you to fix the offer first.

The research he mentions (people trust you more when you admit a bias) and the Eminem rap-battle story are illustrations. He doesn't show his own data for them.

**Verdict:** Hormozi says about 20% monthly churn is average for a paid online community, under 10% is the best, and over 30% is the danger line. Above 30%, fix retention before you work on anything else. He also says don't judge yourself on the blended average. Track churn by how long members have been in, and work on getting them past day 90 and month six.

**Based on:** said it. All of this comes from one talk, "How to Get Your Customers to Stay FOREVER" (March 2026), which is built on Skool platform data.

**The benchmarks**
- "the platform average across School is 80% monthly retention. So said differently, it's 20% churn… Now the best groups have less than 10% churn, aka 90% retention month over month. The not good groups have less than 70% retention, aka 30% or higher." ([@ 1:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=99s))
- He says these numbers fit online, remote and consumer services, not things like insurance premiums or alarm systems ([@ 1:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=65s)).

**When to worry**
- **Over 30% churn.** "if less than seven out of 10 people want to stay on a monthly basis, you probably need to work on your retention more than anything else. It'll be the highest ROI lever." ([@ 1:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=99s))
- **Not just because month one looks bad.** "the biggest rule is that churn drops dramatically with time" ([@ 3:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=199s)). His numbers by tenure:
  - Months one to three: 20% or more.
  - After day 90: "it drops to around 10% or less" ([@ 3:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=233s)).
  - By month six: "it goes from like 10% to 2%."
  
  So "don't overhaul your entire business because your month one churn sucks", unless "basically everyone's leaving, in which case, yes, you should go fix that" ([@ 4:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=264s)).
- **New communities.** If yours is under 90 days old, he says its churn "is always going to be inflated", because nobody has reached the low-churn months yet. It's the same under six months, just less so ([@ 4:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=264s)).

**Why even small gains matter:** going from 20% to 10% churn "you didn't just get a 10 or 12% boost, you got a double in the LTV per customer" ([@ 2:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=133s)).

**What he'd have you do about it**
1. **Count joins and cancels every month.** Label the business growing, flat or declining based on the two numbers ([@ 0:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=33s)).
2. **Plan for month one.** It's the biggest month of churn. His tools are activation, onboarding, setting expectations, selling the right promise and showing up every day ([@ 4:57](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=297s)). Give new members a fast win, ideally within 24 hours.
3. **Day 90 needs a result.** Members should see "some sort of outcome, some sort of change in behavior". Month six "is usually them connecting with other people within that community" ([@ 5:31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=331s)). Get each member one real friend, and introduce new people to about 10 regulars.
4. **Ask why people cancel.** DM everyone who leaves and tag their reason. After about 20 cancels, fix the top one or two reasons. Also ask your longest members why they stay.
5. **Cut what overwhelms people.** He ranks overwhelm as the second biggest cause of churn after price ([@ 9:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=558s)).
6. **Add a discounted annual plan now**, typically about 16–17% off. Annual members only have to decide once, not 12 times, so they churn less ([@ 15:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=952s)).
7. **Show up every day.** Owners who were active in their community every day kept members significantly longer ([@ 13:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=819s)).

**Caveats:**
- All of these numbers come from one source: Skool platform averages that he says came from Sam, Skool's founder. Hormozi is involved with Skool and promotes it.
- His answer would change if your community isn't sold month to month, or isn't an online or consumer service. He says these benchmarks don't apply to things like insurance or alarm systems.

**Verdict:** Pay it off, and do it fast out of profits. Hormozi doesn't see this as a choice between the two, though. The growth moves he'd make first cost little or no cash, so the debt payments shouldn't hold growth back.

**Based on:** he said it. In a May 2026 consult he dealt with almost exactly your situation: a profitable HVAC-cleaning service business doing about $1.25M a year and carrying "about 60,000" in debt ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4)).

**Why he'd say it**
- He leans toward Dave Ramsey on debt: "I tend to skew like very close to the Ramsey side" ([@ 8:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=517s)).
- He gives one reason for it: "Risk when multiplied over a long time horizon tends to come due." Also, "businesses have seasons, they have volatility" ([@ 9:10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=550s)). He asks why people take on debt in the first place, and answers "cuz I wanted to grow faster." He points to Chick-fil-A as an enduring company that runs debt free.
- He admits it's partly about peace of mind: "I'd say this is more of an emotional thing, but it's just this back of mind thing" ([@ 8:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=517s)). He doesn't claim it's a big financial lever.
- It matches one of his recurring rules, which is to get safe first so you can afford risk later: "The first step is that we have to cut all costs, so that we can take more risk" ([@ 0:32](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=32s)).

**What he did:** The owner said he planned to clear the $60k in four to five months. Hormozi replied "Okay, good." He made "continue to pay off the debt" item #2 on the priority list ([@ 30:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=1845s)). Item #1 was a 10% price raise, which he estimated at about 25% more net profit as long as the close rate stays above 65%. In other words, growth came from raising prices, not from holding back cash.

**Where cash for growth does win:** paid ads with proven, measured returns. That client had 13:1 returns on ads, and Hormozi told him to scale spend, possibly from $5k to $30k a month: "if you know that's where the money's coming from, by all means, spend more" ([@ 11:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=681s)). He called that "part of leveling up in business is that you take greater and greater risk" ([@ 11:54](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=714s)). In that consult the ad spend ran alongside the debt payoff. It didn't replace it.

**What would change his answer:** a specific growth use of the cash with returns you've already measured, like that ad account. In that case, fund it and keep paying down the debt. If "growth" means unproven bets, or you can't trace where your customers come from ("then you have a data problem"), he'd say pay off the debt.

One tension: elsewhere he argues that most people take too little risk. In private equity he also describes heavy debt as the way fund managers get rich. He hasn't squared that with his Ramsey-leaning advice for small operating businesses. The vault treats them as different situations, and yours is the small-operating-business one.

If you want to keep this answer, I can save it to `derived/` in the vault.

**Verdict:** No. Hormozi would tell you an 82% close rate means you're underpriced, and he'd raise prices about 10%. You only lose money if your close rate falls below roughly 65%.

At under $3–5M in revenue, he thinks charging more is one of the biggest levers you have. For an ordinary service like duct cleaning, a higher price can raise your close rate, because customers trust more that you'll actually do the job well.

**Based on:** he said it. He has addressed nearly this exact case. In a 2026 consult, Corey, who owns ProShine (an HVAC duct-cleaning company), reported $1.25M in trailing revenue, a 38% net margin and an 82% close rate ([video @ 3:15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=195s)). Your numbers are practically his.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Above 80% is his signal.** "So whenever I hear 80% or over 80% close rates, I usually know that there's room in sale." ([yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4 @ 8:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=486s))
- **His break-even rule.** "As long as we close more than 65%, we make more money." He added that a 10% raise "equals roughly a 25% increase in net profit." (@ 8:06) The math holds for you too, assuming your cost per job stays the same:
  - Today you keep 38¢ of every dollar of price. After a 10% raise you keep 48¢.
  - Break-even close rate is 82% × 38/48 ≈ **65%**.
  - If your close rate holds, profit goes from about $456K to about $576K (+26%).
- **A higher price can mean more closes, not fewer.** "if you raise your prices, what sometimes happens is that the conviction of the customer that you can actually deliver on the promise you're making goes up." ([@ 7:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=420s)) He separates this from luxury goods. In his words, "No one's like bragging at their Rotary Club about how much they spent on their H back." The point is trust that you'll deliver, not status.
- **Owners who stay cheap cost themselves sales.** "they're so afraid of charging money that they actually sell themselves out of a sale" (@ 7:33). A price that's too low makes you look like a "super seedy duct tape operation."
- **The size of business he means:** owners "sub call it three sometimes five million in revenue, some of the biggest levers that exist in the business is simply charging more" (@ 8:06).

**What he's done:** His team had already told Corey he was mispriced for his market. Corey raised prices 23% and the result was "a higher close rate and more money" ([@ 6:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=386s)). Hormozi then made a further 10% raise (to about $1,650 per unit) the first item on Corey's action list ([@ 30:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=1845s)). Almost a year later Corey was projecting $2.3–2.5M. He credited mostly the marketing and lead-flow changes, though, not the price raise.

**What would change his answer:**
- **The close rate drops below 65% after the raise.** He called the 10% "more asking than telling," so it's a test you keep watching.
- **You're no longer underpriced for your market.** His first recommendation rested on comparing Corey with similar businesses. If you're already at the top of local pricing, the 80% signal means less.
- **Your cost per job rises with price.** Then the break-even close rate moves above 65%.

In that same consult, Hormozi said he didn't want to break a business that already works ("no Hail Mary's. This is just consistent yardage." @ 4:19). So it's one measured raise and a watch on the close rate, not a big jump.

One caveat on the source: this video is also an ad for Acquisition.com's consulting, and he cites his own *Offers* book for the theory behind it.

The NASDAQ and IPO equity story isn't Hormozi's. It's told by the host, **Steven Bartlett**, on The Diary of a CEO (E235, 2023-04-03). Hormozi only reacts to it. The transcript is auto-captioned with no speaker labels, so I'm attributing lines from context: the teller says his company "went public on a Stock Exchange in Europe" and later founded "flight story", which is Bartlett's company. That's probably why the wiki doesn't list this story under Hormozi.

**Bartlett's story** ([source @ 1:34:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=2052s))
- **The 4x:** His company was already listed in Europe. While they were considering a second IPO elsewhere, they met 20 investment banks on a road show. The banks told him that "if you move it to the NASDAQ the exact same business would be worth four times more which meant that my net worth would be Forex just by taking the exact same business and moving it to a different Stock Exchange" (the captions mis-transcribe "4x" as "Forex").
- **What he learned:** A skill is only worth as much as the market you apply it to. He looked for "an industry where my skill set was in least Supply but highest demand." For social media marketing and storytelling, that was companies about to IPO, because a good story "can swing your valuation by hundreds of millions" (@ 1:35:17).
- **The equity deal:** After leaving his first company, he worked 9–12 months, "basically freelance", for a company ahead of its IPO, paid in equity. The first one listed at about $3B. "on the day of the IPO the equity that I got for for the 9 to 12 months work that i' done was worth in the region of 7 to8 million" (@ 1:35:51). He gave this as the reason he started Flight Story, which began in the IPO market.

**What Hormozi took from it**
- He agrees straight away ("100% I thoroughly agree with everything you just said") and recasts it as knowing where to fish: "same work yeah same amount of time same Rod more zeros" (@ 1:38:03).
- He adds his own version, conversion-rate work. A 20% lift is worth $200K to a $1M store but $20M to a $100M business. If you take 10% of the value, that's $20K versus $2M, "100x same work". His conclusion: "solve rich people problems they pay better" (@ 1:38:38). This is in the wiki at `wiki/pricing/premium-pricing/sell-to-customers-who-value-it-most.md`.
- He then uses the story as an example of capital as leverage, the step from institutional money to public markets: "you saw like the IPO money like the fact that the NASDAQ was Forex uh the dorf exchange is that where it was right … there's just significantly more capital in that market and so it same work more zeros" (@ 1:45:47). This ties to `wiki/business/leverage/types-of-leverage.md`.

So the story is Bartlett's. Hormozi's part is the principle he draws from it: put the same skill where it's worth the most.

**He didn't, so the question's premise is wrong.** In the vault's only roofing consult, Hormozi told the owner the opposite: go all in on door-to-door. He never said to stop knocking doors, and he never mentioned Google Ads. The only "Google" in the transcript is the owner talking about asking customers for Google reviews.

The source is "How I Would Build a $10M Service Business (If I Had to Start Over)", an episode of his Scale or Fail series ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU)). The owner is Caleb of Keys Roofing in St. Louis. The company was two months old, made about $20K a month, and got its customers from door-knocking and referrals.

**What he actually told him, and why**

- **Door-knocking was already his best channel.** Caleb said he gets a sale for about every 20 doors he knocks. With a small business short on time and money, Hormozi said: "I want to focus all efforts on the highest return stuff that you can do right now." ([@ 3:16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=196s))
- **Being able to go out and get money on demand is rare.** "that reliability of being able to just basically go get money um is something that a lot of entrepreneurs don't know how to do." He compared it to a cat's nine lives: it gives an entrepreneur extra chances to survive. (@ 3:16)
- **Scale what already works instead of trying a new channel.** "Now I think that in terms of scale, you should go all in door to door." ([@ 9:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=589s)) "It's what you're good at." "Like I don't think we need to be cute about this." ([@ 10:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=621s))
- **Grow by hiring a door-to-door sales team and paying them per door.** He worked it out as a 10% commission on a $4K repair, spread over about 50 doors per sale, which comes to roughly $10 per door: "want to go make 10 bucks? Knock that door." "I think you building out this DDD army is like the clear straight shot." ([@ 10:54](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=654s)) "DDD army" is how the auto-captions wrote "D2D", meaning door-to-door.

**What happened next:** At the 90-day follow-up, Hormozi summed up his advice: "the first thing we said was go all in on door to door as primary growth engine." ([@ 24:27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=1467s)) Caleb said he did exactly that, along with the video sales letters (VSLs) and the menu upsell. He reported revenue going from a little under $32K to about $247K. Those are his own numbers, and the video doesn't say whether they're monthly or a running total.

**What would change his answer:** His reasoning rests on the owner already closing reliably at the door. If door-knocking weren't working, or if Caleb's time ran out, "put everything behind your highest-return channel" could point to something else. The vault doesn't record him saying that about this business, though.

If you're thinking of a different video where he did recommend Google Ads, it isn't in this vault yet. Send me the link and I can add it.
